preamble: Voicing of the voiceless uvular stop [q] to the voiced uvular stop [ɢ]. In central and northwestern Iranian Persian (including Tehrani), the letter ق, which stood for Arabic [q] in Early New Persian, merged with غ [ɣ] into one phoneme realized as [ɢ] except in unstressed intervocalic position. Arabic qāf is pronounced [ɢ] in Sudan and in parts of Yemen, and several languages voice /q/ to [ɢ] in voiced surroundings: Lishan Didan (Neo-Aramaic) between a vowel or sonorant and a vowel, and Ket after a nasal. Huánuco Quechua voices Proto-Quechuan *q to [ɢ] in syllable onsets (*isqun > isɢun 'nine').

examples.from: Early New Persian ق [q] (in Arabic loans such as قلب qalb 'heart')
examples.note: A completed phonemic merger: the voiced stop [ɢ] is the default realization, with [ɣ~ʁ] in unstressed intervocalic position. Many other Iranian dialects keep q and ɣ apart.
Some Yemeni dialects realize qāf as the voiced uvular stop.
The literary pronunciation of qāf in Sudan is [ɢ] or [ɡ], even in loans from Modern Standard Arabic; the colloquial reflex is usually velar /ɡ/.
Synchronic voicing: /q/ is realized [ɢ] between a vowel or sonorant and a vowel.

examples.from: /q/ after /ŋ/ in báŋquk 'cave in the ground'
examples.note: Synchronic voicing of /q/ after the velar nasal.
In syllable coda the same phoneme is a fricative (*suqta > suχta 'six', *pusaq > pusaχ 'eight').
